title: An Explainable Sentiment-Informed Approach for Reputational Risk Modelling in Ugandan Government Megaproject Discourse
content: Reputational risk embedded in digital narratives significantly influences stakeholder perceptions of megaprojects, yet computational approaches for its systematic assessment remain limited. This study proposes an explainable sentiment-informed approach that operationalizes reputational risk as a governance-oriented text classification task using weakly supervised discourse analysis. A corpus of 25,480 records was compiled from online news and social media sources related to Ugandan megaprojects and processed using natural language processing techniques. To assess label reliability, three independent annotators evaluated a subset of 2,000 records, yielding an average Cohen's kappa coefficient of 0.7622, indicating substantial agreement. A soft-voting ensemble comprising Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machine classifiers was developed and evaluated. The model achieved an accuracy of 92.37%, a weighted F1-score of 0.9217, and strong agreement with reference labels (Cohen's kappa &gt; 0.80). SHAP-based explainability analysis revealed that governance-sensitive discourse features were the primary drivers of reputational risk predictions, with corruption-related language emerging as the strongest indicator of high-risk narratives. The findings demonstrate the potential of interpretable machine-learning approaches for monitoring reputational risk in governance contexts and supporting evidence-based decision-making in megaproject management.
